mainTopic: Whether one pays נזק for an injury that heals, and whose view the rules of shame payment (בושת) follow
overview: The amud opens by trying to answer רבה's question: if an injury will heal on its own, does the attacker still pay for the damage (נזק)? The גמרא tries a proof from the משנה about a son who hurts a parent without a bruise and still pays all five payments. That case could be deafening, but deafening always causes a bruise. It could be shaving, but the hair may have been removed with a paste so that it never grows back, so the proof fails. The גמרא then notes that אביי and רבא each treated רבה's question as obvious, but in opposite directions, and it adds their related argument about injuring an עבד עברי. Next, the גמרא shows that the משנה's rule on shame payment (בושת) follows רבי שמעון, not רבי מאיר or רבי יהודה. Finally, it looks at a ברייתא about someone who meant to shame one person and shamed another. That ברייתא seems to fit no תנא, and the גמרא answers that it can follow רבי יהודה or even רבי מאיר. The question of whether a child can be shamed is answered with רב פפא's teaching, and the discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The משנה seems to answer רבה's question
steps.stepSummary: The משנה ends with 'liable for all of them.' The גמרא argues that hurting a parent without a bruise must mean an injury that will heal, and he still pays everything.
steps.simpleTranslation: [The משנה concludes:] He is liable for all of them. Now, this case of 'he did not make a bruise on him,' what does it look like? Isn't it a case where he hit him on his hand and it will eventually heal? And still the משנה teaches: he is liable for all of them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting the משנה and then uses it to try to answer רבה's question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the son had made a bruise, he would be put to death for hitting a parent, so the משנה must be talking about a hit with no bruise. The גמרא assumes such a hit is the kind that heals by itself, like a hand that recovers. Since the משנה still requires all five payments, including נזק, this seems to show that you pay for נזק even when the injury will heal.

keyTerms.meaning: Liable for all of them, meaning all five payments for injury
A bruise or wound where blood gathers or comes out
What are the circumstances? What does this case look like?
It will eventually go back to how it was, meaning it will heal

steps.confusionAlert: 'All of them' refers to the five payments for injury: נזק, צער, ריפוי, שבת and בושת. It does not refer to a list of different people.

phrases.english: He is liable for all of them.
phrases.notes: 'All of them' means the five payments, from the משנה quoted just before this.

phrases.aramaic: הַאי ״לֹא עָשָׂה בּוֹ חַבּוּרָה״, הֵיכִי דָּמֵי?
phrases.english: This case of 'he did not make a bruise on him,' what are its circumstances?
Isn't it a case where he hit him on his hand
and it will eventually go back to normal?
And yet it teaches: he is liable for all of them!
phrases.notes: So he pays נזק even though the hand will heal. That would answer רבה's question.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי לֹא עָשָׂה בּוֹ חַבּוּרָה הֵיכִי דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the משנה quoted earlier and draws a proof from it for רבה's question.
steps.raayaObject: רבה's question: whether a person pays נזק for an injury that will heal on its own
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה: one who hurts his parent without a חבורה is liable for all five payments

steps.title: Maybe the משנה is about deafening
steps.stepSummary: The proof is pushed away. The case may be one where the son deafened his parent without a bruise, and deafness never heals.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: Here we are dealing with a case where he deafened him, and he did not make a bruise on him.
steps.whatsHappening: Someone rejects the proof by suggesting a different case for the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Deafness is permanent, so paying נזק in that case is obvious and tells us nothing about an injury that heals. The משנה can therefore be explained without touching רבה's question at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, what are we dealing with? This introduces a narrower case.

phrases.english: They say: Here, what are we dealing with?

phrases.aramaic: כְּגוֹן שֶׁחֵירְשׁוֹ, וְלֹא עָשָׂה בּוֹ חַבּוּרָה.
phrases.english: A case where he deafened him, and did not make a bruise on him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 1 by giving the משנה a case of permanent damage.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the assumption that 'no bruise' must mean an injury that heals.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא could be about deafness, which is permanent, so it proves nothing about injuries that heal.

steps.title: Deafening always involves a bruise
steps.stepSummary: The deafness answer is challenged using רבה's own teaching: deafening a father is a capital crime because it always causes a bruise inside the ear.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't רבה say: One who deafens his father is put to death, because it is impossible to deafen without a bruise. A drop of blood fell into his ear!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the suggestion that the ברייתא is about deafening.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה teaches that deafening always comes with a bruise, even if it cannot be seen, because blood drips inside the ear. A son who bruises his parent is put to death, not made to pay. So deafening cannot be the case of the משנה, which is about a son who makes no bruise and pays money.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't he say? This introduces a challenge from a known statement.

phrases.english: But didn't רבה say:
One who deafened his father is put to death,
phrases.notes: The printed גמרא has the word in round brackets. The corrected wording uses the word in square brackets. Both mean deafening.

phrases.english: because it is impossible
to deafen without a bruise;
a drop of blood fell into his ear!
phrases.notes: The bruise is inside the ear, so you may not see it from outside.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Knocks down the deafness case suggested in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion that the ברייתא is about deafening without a bruise
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: According to רבה, deafening without a bruise is impossible. Deafening a parent would then bring the death penalty, not payments, so it cannot be the ברייתא's case.

steps.title: The case is shaving, and hair grows back
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא settles on a case of shaving the parent's hair with no bruise. Hair grows back, which is exactly רבה's question, so the proof works again.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, here we are dealing with a case where he shaved him. If he shaved him, the hair grows back, and that is exactly our question!
steps.whatsHappening: With deafening ruled out, the גמרא gives a new case for the ברייתא. That case brings the proof for רבה's question back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Shaving causes no bruise, so the son is not put to death and pays money instead. Hair grows back, so this is an injury that heals, just like the hand in רבה's question. Since the ברייתא still says he pays everything, it again seems to show that you pay נזק even for damage that heals.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. This drops the last idea and offers a new one.
That he shaved him, cutting off his hair
It surely comes back, meaning the hair grows back
And this is exactly our question

steps.whatToRemember: After deafening is ruled out, the best case left for the משנה is shaving. Hair grows back, so the משנה once again seems to answer רבה's question: you pay נזק even for damage that heals.

phrases.english: Rather, here, what are we dealing with?
A case where he shaved him.
If he shaved him, it surely grows back,
and that is exactly our question!
phrases.notes: 'Our question' is רבה's question about an injury that will heal.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן כְּגוֹן שֶׁגִּילְּחוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 3 ruled out deafening, this gives the ברייתא a new case that brings back the proof from step 1.
steps.raayaObject: רבה's question: whether a person pays נזק for an injury that will heal
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא, now read as being about shaving a parent's hair without a bruise, still requires all five payments

steps.title: Maybe the hair was removed with a paste and will never grow back
steps.stepSummary: The shaving proof is pushed away. The case may involve a hair-removing paste, so the hair does not return.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answer: maybe the case is where the son smeared his parent with a hair-removing paste, and the hair never grows back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the proof from Step 4 by offering a different case where the damage is permanent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 needed an injury with no bruise that heals, which is why it chose shaving. Here the גמרא says the son may have used a paste that kills the hair roots. Then the damage is permanent, and the ברייתא tells us nothing about an injury that heals, which is רבה's question.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, what case are we dealing with? (introduces a narrower case)

phrases.english: They say: Here, what case are we dealing with?
Such as where he smeared him with a hair-removing paste,
so the hair does not come back.
phrases.notes: This is the key point. If it never grows back, the injury is permanent, so it can't answer רבה's question about an injury that heals.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the shaving proof of Step 4 by suggesting a permanent-damage case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof that one pays everything even for an injury that heals.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא could be talking about permanent hair loss from a paste, not hair that grows back.

steps.title: How all five payments fit the paste case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that pain, medical costs, lost work, and shame all apply when the hair is removed with a paste.
steps.simpleTranslation: Pain: he has cracks on his scalp and cries out from them. Medical costs: he needs treatment. Lost work: he used to dance in taverns using head motions, and now the cracks stop him. Shame: there is no greater shame than this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the new case by showing that the ברייתא's words 'liable for all of them' really fit it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone could ask how a no-bruise paste injury could involve all five payments. The גמרא describes cracks on the scalp from the paste. These cause pain, need treatment, and stop him from working as a dancer, and losing one's hair is a deep shame. This keeps the case from Step 5 standing.

keyTerms.meaning: Cracks or sores on the scalp

phrases.english: Pain: because he has cracks on his head,
and he cries out because of those cracks.
phrases.notes: Some versions include the word in square brackets and some don't. The meaning stays the same.

phrases.english: Medical costs: because he needs to be treated.
Lost work: because he used to dance in taverns,
where he has to make all kinds of motions with his head;
and now he cannot make those motions because of those cracks.

phrases.aramaic: בּוֹשֶׁת – אֵין לְךָ בּוֹשֶׁת גָּדוֹל מִזֶּה.
phrases.english: Shame: there is no greater shame than this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the paste case of Step 5 by showing it fits 'liable for all of them.'
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A no-bruise paste injury might seem unable to involve pain, medical costs and lost work.
steps.terutzMaskana: The paste causes scalp cracks, so all the payments apply.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה can be explained as a case of permanent hair loss, so it does not answer רבה's question about an injury that heals.

steps.title: רבה's open question was decided by אביי and רבא in opposite ways
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that what רבה asked about was obvious to אביי one way and to רבא the other way.
steps.simpleTranslation: The matter that רבה was unsure about was obvious to אביי in one direction and to רבא in the other direction.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves the משנה behind and makes a new comment. It sets up the next step, which brings the argument that shows this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה asked whether someone who causes an injury that will heal must pay full value. The גמרא says that אביי and רבא did not see this as a question. Each was sure of the answer, but they disagreed.

keyTerms.meaning: To this side, in this direction

phrases.english: And the matter that רבה was unsure about,
was obvious to אביי in this direction,
and to רבא in that direction.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from the משנה fails, the גמרא points out where the question was actually decided.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אביי and רבא each held a clear but opposite answer to רבה's question.

steps.title: The weakened hand that will heal
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the attacker pays both big and small lost-work payments even though the hand will heal. רבא says he pays only for each day of lost work.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: if someone hit another person's hand and it became weak, but it will recover, אביי says he pays both the big lost-work payment and the small lost-work payment. רבא says he pays only for the work missed each day.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the argument that proves what it said in Step 7.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'big' lost-work payment is the drop in the person's value because of the weak hand. The 'small' one is the work he misses while he recovers. אביי makes him pay the big amount even though the hand will heal, so for him the answer to רבה is 'pay in full.' רבא says to pay only day by day, so for him it is 'not in full.'

keyTerms.meaning: The big lost-work payment: the loss in his value
The small lost-work payment: the days of work he misses

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think שבת here only means missed workdays. The 'big' שבת is the drop in his overall value, as if the hand were damaged for good.

phrases.english: As it was taught: if he hit him on his hand and it became weak,
but it will eventually recover,

phrases.aramaic: אַבָּיֵי אָמַר: נוֹתֵן לוֹ שֶׁבֶת גְּדוֹלָה
phrases.english: אביי said: He gives him the big lost-work payment,
phrases.notes: He means the drop in the person's value because of a weak hand, as if he were sold in the market.

phrases.english: and the small lost-work payment.
And רבא said: He does not give him anything

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא דְּמֵי שִׁבְתּוֹ שֶׁבְּכׇל יוֹם וָיוֹם.
phrases.english: except the value of his lost work for each and every day.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source behind Step 7's claim.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that אביי and רבא each settled רבה's question in opposite ways.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The argument between אביי and רבא about a weakened hand that will heal.
steps.whyThisMatters: This argument answers the main question of the whole discussion: whether an injury that will heal is paid as if it were permanent.

steps.title: Cutting off the hand of someone else's עבד עברי
steps.stepSummary: אביי splits the payment: the big lost-work payment to the slave and the small one to the master. רבא gives everything to the slave, who buys land with it, and the master eats the produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: if someone cuts off the hand of another person's עבד עברי, אביי says the big lost-work payment goes to the slave and the small one goes to the master. רבא says everything is given to the slave, land is bought with it, and the master eats the produce.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second argument between אביי and רבא, this time about who gets the money when an עבד עברי is injured.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An עבד עברי belongs to his master only for a limited time and then goes free. אביי gives the permanent loss of value to the slave, and the missed work during his years of service to the master. רבא says not to split it. All the money goes to the slave and buys land, and the master enjoys its produce while the slave works for him.

keyTerms.meaning: A Jewish servant who serves for a limited time
Eats the produce, enjoys the profits

steps.whatToRemember: אביי and רבא argue about a healing injury and also about splitting payment for an עבד עברי. For the slave, אביי divides the money, while רבא keeps it all with the slave and gives the master only the produce.

phrases.aramaic: אִיתְּמַר: הַקּוֹטֵעַ יַד עֶבֶד עִבְרִי שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ –
phrases.english: It was taught: one who cuts off the hand of another person's Jewish servant,

phrases.aramaic: אַבָּיֵי אָמַר: נוֹתֵן לוֹ שֶׁבֶת גְּדוֹלָה לָעֶבֶד,
phrases.english: אביי said: He gives the big lost-work payment to the servant,
and the small lost-work payment to the master.
רבא said: Everything is given to the servant,
and land is bought with the money,
and the master eats the produce.
phrases.notes: He means while the servant is still serving him. After that, the land and its produce belong to the servant.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר: הַקּוֹטֵעַ יַד עֶבֶד עִבְרִי שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings another argument between the same two אמוראים, using the same terms big and small lost work.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אביי: divide the payments between the slave and the master. רבא: all goes to the slave to buy land, and the master eats the produce.

steps.title: When the injury hurts only the slave, not the master
steps.stepSummary: If the injury lowers the slave's value only for himself, such as a cut ear-tip or nostril-tip, all the payment goes to the slave. If it also lowers his value for the master, it is the מחלוקת of אביי and רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is obvious: if he lowered the slave's value for the slave himself but not for his master, all the money goes to the slave. When does that happen? When he split the tip of the ear or the tip of the nose. If he lowered the value for the master, that is the argument of אביי and רבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the slave discussion by sorting cases into two groups: damage that matters only to the slave, and damage that also affects the master.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A cut ear-tip or nose-tip does not stop the slave from working, so the master loses nothing and the slave gets everything. Only when the master's use of the slave is hurt does the split between master and slave come up. That is exactly where אביי and רבא argued in step 9.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How does this happen?

steps.whatToRemember: Injury that hurts only the slave: everything goes to the slave. Injury that hurts the master too: אביי and רבא argue about how to split it.

phrases.english: It is obvious: if he lowered the slave's value for the slave himself,
but did not lower it for his master,
What is such a case?
phrases.notes: This is a quick side question in the middle of the sentence. The main sentence picks up again at row 6.

phrases.english: Where he split the tip of his ear
or the tip of his nostril.
Then all of the payment goes to the slave himself.
If he lowered the slave's value for his master,
that is the dispute of אביי and רבא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Marks out where the אביי and רבא dispute from step 9 applies and where it does not.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Damage that matters only to the slave goes entirely to the slave. The master and slave split the payment only when the master's use of the slave is harmed.

steps.title: Whose view is the משנה on shame payment?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה that shame is measured by who did the shaming and who was shamed, and asks which תנא holds this.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shame: it all depends on the one who shames and the one who is shamed. Whose view is our משנה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic. It quotes the משנה's rule about בושת and asks whose opinion it follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says the shame payment changes with the people involved. The גמרא wants to know which תנא agrees with that, because the תנאים disagree about how shame is measured.

keyTerms.meaning: Shame or embarrassment, one of the five payments for injury

phrases.english: Shame: it all depends on the one who shames and the one who is shamed.
Whose view is our משנה?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section on the בושת part of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא holds that shame payment depends on both people involved?

steps.title: It is רבי שמעון, not רבי מאיר or רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers right away: the משנה follows רבי שמעון.
steps.simpleTranslation: Not רבי מאיר and not רבי יהודה. Rather, it is רבי שמעון.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states its answer first: the משנה is רבי שמעון. It will explain why in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer comes before the reasons. Next the גמרא quotes the ברייתא that lays out all three views (step 13) and shows why the other two do not fit (steps 14 and 15).

phrases.aramaic: לָא רַבִּי מֵאִיר וְלָא רַבִּי יְהוּדָה,
phrases.english: It is not רבי מאיר and not רבי יהודה,
rather, it is רבי שמעון.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא רַבִּי מֵאִיר וְלָא רַבִּי יְהוּדָה, אֶלָּא רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 11.

steps.title: The ברייתא with three views on measuring shame
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר treats every Jew as a noble who lost his money. רבי יהודה measures each person by his own standing. רבי שמעון treats the rich as nobles who lost their money and the poor as the lowest among them.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned: all of them are viewed as free people of standing who lost their property, because they are children of אברהם, יצחק and יעקב. These are the words of רבי מאיר. רבי יהודה says: the great by his greatness, the small by his smallness. רבי שמעון says: the rich are viewed as free people of standing who lost their property, and the poor as the lowest among them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the ברייתא that lays out the three opinions. It will use this to decide whose view the משנה is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר uses one level for everyone, so a person's own standing does not matter. רבי יהודה goes fully by each person's standing. רבי שמעון takes a middle path with two levels, one for the rich and one for the poor.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי שמעון does not judge each person one by one like רבי יהודה. He uses only two levels: rich and poor.

phrases.english: As we learned: and all of them

phrases.aramaic: רוֹאִין אוֹתָן כְּאִילּוּ הֵם בְּנֵי חוֹרִין
phrases.english: are viewed as if they were free people of standing
who lost their property,
because they are children of אברהם, יצחק and יעקב.
These are the words of רבי מאיר.
רבי יהודה says:

phrases.aramaic: הַגָּדוֹל לְפִי גּוֹדְלוֹ, וְהַקָּטָן לְפִי קׇטְנוֹ.
phrases.english: The great person according to his greatness, and the small person according to his smallness.
רבי שמעון says: rich people

phrases.aramaic: רוֹאִין אוֹתָן כְּאִילּוּ הֵם בְּנֵי חוֹרִין שֶׁיָּרְדוּ מִנִּכְסֵיהֶם,
phrases.english: are viewed as if they were free people of standing who lost their property;
poor people are viewed like the lowest among them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source that shows the three views behind the answer in step 12.
steps.raayaObject: That the משנה matches רבי שמעון.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא recording the views of רבי מאיר, רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון on measuring shame.

steps.title: Why the משנה cannot be רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says shame depends on the people involved, but רבי מאיר treats everyone the same, so the משנה is not his view.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view is it? Now, if it were רבי מאיר: the משנה teaches that it all depends on the one who shames and the one who is shamed, but for רבי מאיר everyone is equal!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts proving its answer by ruling out רבי מאיר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה clearly expects different amounts for different people. רבי מאיר gives everyone one level, so he cannot be the author of this משנה.

phrases.english: Whose view is it?
Now, if it were רבי מאיר,
our משנה teaches:
it all depends on the one who shames and the one who is shamed;

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי מֵאִיר – כּוּלְּהוּ בַּהֲדֵי הֲדָדֵי נִינְהוּ!
phrases.english: but for רבי מאיר, they are all equal to one another!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the ברייתא from step 13 to rule out רבי מאיר.
steps.raayaObject: That the משנה is not רבי מאיר.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's wording compared with רבי מאיר's single level for everyone.

steps.title: Why the משנה cannot be רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: A משנה rules that shaming a blind person makes one liable, but רבי יהודה says a blind person has no בושת, so the משנה is not his view.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it were רבי יהודה: the משנה teaches that one who shames a blind person must pay, while רבי יהודה says a blind person has no shame payment!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rules out רבי יהודה by pointing to another ruling in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'great by his greatness' line on its own could fit the משנה. But the משנה also makes one pay for shaming a blind person, and רבי יהודה exempts that case. So the משנה cannot be רבי יהודה either.

phrases.english: And if it were רבי יהודה,

phrases.aramaic: מַתְנִיתִין קָתָנֵי: הַמְבַיֵּישׁ אֶת הַסּוֹמֵא – חַיָּיב;
phrases.english: the משנה teaches: one who shames a blind person is liable;
phrases.notes: This ruling comes from a little later in the same משנה.

phrases.english: whereas רבי יהודה says:
A blind person has no shame payment!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second part of the proof: after ruling out רבי מאיר, it now rules out רבי יהודה.
steps.raayaObject: That the משנה is not רבי יהודה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's ruling about a blind person compared with רבי יהודה's view that a blind person has no בושת.

steps.title: So the משנה must be רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: With רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה ruled out, the משנה must follow רבי שמעון.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, isn't it רבי שמעון?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the process of elimination: the only view left is רבי שמעון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון's two levels, rich and poor, fit the משנה's statement that shame depends on the people involved. So the answer given in step 12 is now proven.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's rule on shame payment follows רבי שמעון: rich people are treated as nobles who lost their money, and poor people as the lowest of the poor.

phrases.english: Rather, isn't it רבי שמעון?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion after the two views were ruled out in steps 14 and 15.

steps.title: Maybe the משנה can follow רבי יהודה after all
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on Step 15. It suggests that when רבי יהודה said a blind person has no בושת, he only meant that a blind person does not pay for shaming others. He still gets paid when someone shames him.
steps.simpleTranslation: You could even say the משנה follows רבי יהודה. When he said a blind person has no shame, he meant we don't take payment from the blind person. But we do give payment to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from Step 15. It offers a new reading of רבי יהודה that fits the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 said: the משנה makes someone who shames a blind person pay, and רבי יהודה says a blind person has no בושת, so the משנה cannot be his view. Now the גמרא splits רבי יהודה's rule into two directions. A blind person does not pay when he shames others, but he does collect when others shame him. If that is right, the משנה and רבי יהודה no longer clash.

keyTerms.meaning: You can even say: a formula that opens a defense of a view that seemed ruled out
To take from him (to make him pay)
To give to him (to pay him)

phrases.english: You can even say it is רבי יהודה.
When רבי יהודה said
a blind person has no shame,
that is about taking payment from him.
phrases.notes: He means: if the blind person shames someone else, he doesn't have to pay.

phrases.english: But as for giving payment to him,
we do give it to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in Step 15 that ruled out רבי יהודה
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the blind-person case that the משנה is not רבי יהודה
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It assumed רבי יהודה's rule works in both directions, when it may only mean a blind person does not pay

steps.title: The end of the משנה shows the blind person is treated the same both ways
steps.stepSummary: The end of that משנה lists only a sleeping person as exempt when he shames someone. It does not list a blind person. So the משנה must hold that a blind person is treated the same in both directions, against Step 17's reading of רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the end of the משנה teaches: one who shames a sleeping person must pay, and a sleeping person who shames someone is exempt. It does not teach that a blind person who shames someone is exempt. This shows there is no difference either way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks Step 17's defense, using the end of the same משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a blind person were exempt when he shames others, the משנה would have listed him next to the sleeping person who is exempt. Since it lists only the sleeping person, the משנה must hold that a blind person who shames someone does pay. That cuts against the two-way split suggested for רבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: The end part of a משנה or ברייתא
By implication, from this we learn

phrases.english: But from the fact that the end part teaches:
One who shames a sleeping person must pay,
and a sleeping person who shamed someone is exempt;
and it does not teach:
a blind person who shamed someone is exempt;
this shows there is no difference this way
and no difference that way!
phrases.notes: He means: whether the blind person shames or gets shamed, whoever did the shaming pays.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the defense of רבי יהודה given in Step 17
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the משנה can follow רבי יהודה because a blind person only fails to pay but does collect
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's silence about a blind person being exempt, right next to the sleeping person who is exempt, shows that a blind person who shames someone does pay

steps.title: It is clear the משנה follows רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: Since the defense of רבי יהודה failed, the גמרא confirms that the משנה is רבי שמעון.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is clear: our משנה is רבי שמעון.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes this back-and-forth and returns firmly to its conclusion from Step 16.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר was ruled out in Step 14. The attempt to save רבי יהודה was knocked down in Step 18. That leaves only רבי שמעון, who treats people differently by their standing and gives a blind person בושת.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, it is clear: a formula for a firm conclusion

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה about payment for shame follows רבי שמעון: rich people are treated like nobles who lost their money, poor people like the lowest among them, and a blind person does have בושת.

phrases.english: Rather, it is clear:
our משנה is רבי שמעון.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מְחַוַּורְתָּא מַתְנִיתִין רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Concludes after the challenge in Step 18 defeats the defense of רבי יהודה

steps.title: A ברייתא about shaming the wrong person that seems to match no one
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: if someone meant to shame a small person but shamed a great one, he pays the great one what he would have owed the small one. The same goes for meaning to shame a slave but shaming a free man. The גמרא asks whose view this is and claims it fits none of the three תנאים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who taught what the רבנן taught? If someone meant to shame a small person and shamed a great person, he gives the great person the payment for the small person's shame. If he meant to shame a slave and shamed a free man, he gives the free man the payment for a slave's shame. Whose view is this? Not רבי מאיר, not רבי יהודה, and not רבי שמעון!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic. It brings a ברייתא and claims it does not fit any of the three תנאים we just learned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the person who did the shaming pays, but only at the lower rate of the person he meant to shame. The גמרא puts this ruling up against the three views from Step 13 and says none of them can produce it. The reasons come in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: Who is the תנא who taught this?

phrases.english: Who taught this
that the Rabbis taught:
If he meant to shame the small person
and shamed the great person,
he gives the great person
the payment for the small person's shame.
If he meant to shame the slave
and shamed a free man,
he gives the free man
the payment for the slave's shame.
Whose view is this?
Not רבי מאיר,

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא רַבִּי יְהוּדָה, וְלָא רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן!
phrases.english: and not רבי יהודה, and not רבי שמעון!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new discussion that uses the three views from Step 13
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא the ברייתא about shaming the wrong person follows, given that it seems to fit none of them

steps.title: The working assumption: small and great mean poor and rich
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא states the assumption behind its question: in the ברייתא, the small person means someone poor and the great person means someone rich.
steps.simpleTranslation: You are thinking that small means small in property and great means great in property.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא tells us how it is reading the ברייתא before it explains why no תנא fits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words קטן and גדול could mean several things. Here the גמרא reads them as poor and rich, so the ברייתא is about different levels of payment based on wealth. The phrase קא סלקא דעתך signals that this is the current assumption.

keyTerms.meaning: You are thinking, it enters your mind: introduces an assumption

phrases.english: You are thinking:
small means small in property,
great means great in property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reading of the ברייתא that the claim in Step 20 rests on
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the ברייתא, קטן is taken to mean a poor person and גדול a rich person.

steps.title: Why each of the three תנאים cannot fit the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר treats everyone as equal, so there would be no lower rate for a small person. רבי יהודה says slaves have no בושת at all. רבי שמעון says someone who meant to shame one person and shamed another is fully exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is רבי מאיר, he says they are all equal to each other! If it is רבי יהודה, he says slaves have no shame! If it is רבי שמעון, he says: if he meant to shame this one and shamed that one, he is exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its claim from Step 20 by showing exactly how the ברייתא clashes with each of the three תנאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי מאיר, poor and rich get the same payment, so 'paying the small person's rate' makes no sense. For רבי יהודה, a slave gets nothing, so there is no 'slave's rate' to pay. For רבי שמעון, shaming the wrong person brings no payment at all, while the ברייתא makes him pay.

keyTerms.meaning: They are all equal to one another
Slaves have no payment for shame

steps.confusionAlert: Each תנא is ruled out for a different reason. רבי מאיר clashes with the small/great part, רבי יהודה with the slave part, and רבי שמעון with the wrong-person part of the ברייתא.

phrases.english: If it is רבי מאיר, doesn't he say:
they are all equal to one another!
And if it is רבי יהודה, doesn't he say:
slaves have no shame!
And if it is רבי שמעון, doesn't he say:
if he meant to shame this one
and shamed that one, he is exempt!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the claim in Step 20 using the assumption from Step 21
steps.raayaObject: That the ברייתא follows none of the three תנאים
steps.raayaSupportSource: The known views: רבי מאיר treats everyone as equal, רבי יהודה says slaves have no בושת, and רבי שמעון exempts one who shamed the wrong person

steps.title: Why רבי שמעון requires intent for the specific person
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון learns בושת from killing. A killer is liable only if he meant to kill that person, and the same is true for shaming.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why does רבי שמעון say this? Shaming is like killing. A killer is not liable unless he aimed at that person, as the פסוק says 'he lies in wait for him and rises up against him.' Shaming too is not liable unless he aimed at that person, as the פסוק says 'she put forth her hand and took hold of his private parts.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the source for רבי שמעון's rule from Step 22. This finishes the proof that the ברייתא cannot be רבי שמעון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The killing פסוק says 'lies in wait for him,' which points to a specific target. The גמרא compares shaming to killing and reads the בושת פסוק the same way. Since killing needs intent toward that very person, shaming does too. So under רבי שמעון, someone who meant to shame one person and shamed another pays nothing at all, while the ברייתא makes him pay something.

keyTerms.meaning: He intends it for him, aiming at that specific person
His private parts; the root of the word בושת

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the three-way problem from Step 20 is real. רבי שמעון is ruled out for a clear reason based on a פסוק.

phrases.english: What is the reason? It is like killing;
just as with killing, he is not liable until he intends it for him,
as it is written: 'And he lies in wait for him and rises up against him'
meaning, not until he intends it for him;
shaming too, he is not liable until he intends it for him,
as it is written: 'And she put forth her hand and took hold of his private parts'
meaning, not until he intends it for him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for רבי שמעון's position cited in Step 22.
steps.raayaObject: רבי שמעון's rule that a person who meant to shame one person and shamed another is fully exempt.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A comparison to killing: 'וְאָרַב לוֹ' (דברים 19:11) and 'וְהֶחֱזִיקָה בִּמְבֻשָׁיו' (דברים 25:11).

steps.title: The ברייתא can be רבי יהודה: slaves' shame is used for measuring
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה only means slaves are not paid for בושת. Their בושת can still be valued as a measuring stick.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, the ברייתא is רבי יהודה. When רבי יהודה says slaves have no בושת, he means we do not pay them. But to put a value on something, we do value their בושת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 20 by saying the ברייתא follows רבי יהודה after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 22 assumed that under רבי יהודה a slave's בושת is worth nothing, so there is nothing to measure. The גמרא now splits the idea: a slave gets no payment, but the court can still figure out how much his בושת would be worth. So a man who meant to shame a slave and shamed a free man pays the free man that slave-level amount.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, actually; used to keep an original position
To give to them, to pay them
To put a value on, to appraise

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יהודה is not saying slaves suddenly get paid. The slave still receives nothing. Only the free man who was actually shamed gets paid, using the slave's value as the rate.

phrases.english: Really, it is רבי יהודה,
and when רבי יהודה said:
'Slaves have no בושת,' that is about giving payment to them;
but for putting a value on something, we do appraise with them.
phrases.notes: He means the slave's בושת is used to set the amount owed to the free man who was actually shamed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 20 by removing the objection to רבי יהודה raised in Step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing a ruling: רבי יהודה's statement only refers to payment, not to valuing.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Under רבי יהודה a slave's בושת is zero, so it cannot be used as a rate for the free man.
steps.terutzMaskana: A slave is not paid for בושת, but his בושת can be valued, so the ברייתא fits רבי יהודה.

steps.title: The ברייתא can even be רבי מאיר: a real child and a real adult
steps.stepSummary: 'Small' and 'great' in the ברייתא do not mean poor and rich. They mean a real child and a real adult, so even רבי מאיר can agree.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or if you like, say it is even רבי מאיר. Do you think 'great' means great in property and 'small' means small in property? No. 'Great' means an actual adult and 'small' means an actual child.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second answer to Step 20, showing the ברייתא can follow רבי מאיר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 21 assumed small and great meant poor and rich, and רבי מאיר treats poor and rich the same. Now the גמרא reads small and great as child and adult. רבי מאיר's equality rule is about wealth, so a child's lower level of shame can still make a difference.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you like, say; introduces a second answer

phrases.english: And if you like, say:
you can even say it is רבי מאיר.
Do you think 'great' means great in property,
and 'small' means small in property?
No; 'great' means an actual adult,
and 'small' means an actual child.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא רַבִּי מֵאִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate answer to Step 20, this time defending רבי מאיר instead of רבי יהודה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: changing what 'small' and 'great' mean.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Small and great mean poor and rich, which רבי מאיר treats as equal.
steps.terutzMaskana: Small and great mean child and adult, so the ברייתא can fit רבי מאיר.

steps.title: Can a child be shamed at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the new reading: does a child even have בושת?
steps.simpleTranslation: But does a child have בושת at all?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from Step 25.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a child cannot feel shame, there is no 'child amount' to use as a rate. Then the second answer, that the ברייתא is רבי מאיר, would fall apart.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone who is subject to shame, who can be shamed

phrases.english: But is a child someone who can be shamed?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reading of 'small' as an actual child given in Step 25.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 25 that 'small' in the ברייתא means a real child.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A child may not understand shame, so he would have no בושת at all to use as a rate.

steps.title: Yes, a child who feels it when embarrassed
steps.stepSummary: Using רב פפא's teaching, a child who feels embarrassed when people embarrass him does have בושת.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes. As רב פפא said, this is a child who, when people embarrass him, feels embarrassed. Here too...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge of Step 26 by bringing a teaching of רב פפא. The sentence continues in the next line of the גמרא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Not every child counts, only one old enough to feel hurt when shamed. Such a child has real בושת, so his amount can serve as the rate, and the answer that the ברייתא is רבי מאיר stands.

phrases.english: Yes; as רב פפא said:
a child who, when they embarrass him, feels embarrassed;
here too...

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Case detailing: the קטן in the ברייתא is a child old enough to feel embarrassment.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A child cannot feel shame, so there is no child-level בושת to use as the rate, and the answer that the ברייתא is רבי מאיר falls.
steps.terutzMaskana: A child who feels embarrassed when people embarrass him has בושת, following רב פפא, so the reading of קטן as an actual child stands.
